question: Today a British mince pie is a sweet pastry full of raisins and spice. But centuries ago, what was actually minced to go inside it?
source_excerpt: Meat was gradually dropped over the nineteenth century, so modern mincemeat contains dried fruit, nuts, apples, spices, and brandy or vinegar, but no meat.

extra.why_interesting: Players treat a mince pie as a sweet fruit pastry and never question the name; realising 'mince' literally meant chopped meat is a satisfying 'of course' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Mince pies historically contained minced meat (beef, mutton, tongue, pork) plus suet, dropped gradually in the 19th century, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mince_pie

explanation: Early mince pies held chopped mutton or beef cooked with fruit and spices. The meat slowly vanished, but the beef fat called suet still turns up in many mincemeat recipes.

question: In Britain, families mix their Christmas pudding on 'Stir-up Sunday'. But the name doesn't come from the pudding. It comes from the first words of what?
source_excerpt: Stir up, we beseech thee, O Lord, the wills of thy faithful people...

extra.why_interesting: Everyone assumes the name describes stirring the pudding batter; in fact the pudding custom borrowed its name from the opening words of a church prayer.
extra.verification_notes: Stir-up Sunday is named for the opening words of the collect ('Stir up, we beseech thee, O Lord...') in the Book of Common Prayer, which is a church prayer.

explanation: The prayer read in Anglican churches that Sunday begins 'Stir up, we beseech thee, O Lord'. It fell on just the right weekend to give the puddings a few weeks to mature, so the name stuck to the kitchen.

question: Eggnog once caused a real riot. Cadets at America's most famous army academy smuggled in whiskey for their Christmas eggnog, and the party went badly wrong. Which academy?
source_excerpt: A drunken Christmas eggnog party in the North Barracks grew into a riot that lasted until Christmas morning and involved more than a third of the cadets.

extra.why_interesting: Eggnog is the cosy, harmless Christmas drink, and military academies stand for discipline. The clash is funny, and 'America's most famous army school' gives a reachable path to the name.
extra.verification_notes: The Eggnog Riot of 24–25 December 1826 occurred at the US Military Academy at West Point after cadets smuggled in whiskey for their Christmas eggnog.

explanation: Alcohol was banned, so cadets sneaked in several gallons of whiskey. By Christmas morning they were smashing windows, and around twenty cadets were court-martialled.

question: Long before they held paper hats and bad jokes, the very first Christmas crackers in Victorian London were just a twist of paper wrapped around what?
alternative_answers: a sweet with a love message
source_excerpt: he came across the French 'bonbon', a sugared almond wrapped in a twist of tissue paper.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a cracker as a paper tube holding a hat, a bad joke and a plastic toy, and assume that was always it. In fact the whole thing started as fancy sweet wrapping, and the bang, hat and toy were added later. The twisted-end shape is a clue a player can reason from, because it looks like a wrapped sweet.
extra.verification_notes: Tom Smith's original product was a French-style bonbon (sugared almond/sweet) in a twist of tissue paper, later adapted into the cracker, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Smith_(confectioner).

explanation: London confectioner Tom Smith copied the French bonbon, a sugared almond in twisted paper. He later added a love note and then the bang, reportedly inspired by the crackle of a log fire.
